1:
When this instruction reached Moses nobody can fix. Gill admits the date is uncertain, guessing it belongs to the settling of the camps, and noting that it stands recorded here because marching was among the purposes these instruments served. Ellicott raises a sharper question about their novelty. Leviticus already mentions a jubilee trumpet, from which some infer that silver pairs existed before; but the earlier passage uses shophar, whereas hazozerah — the term employed here — surfaces for the first time in this verse. He grants that the opening clause could be rendered "now the Lord had spoken", yet the vocabulary tells against reading these as older equipment.

Shape and workmanship are described from several directions. Ellicott corrects "of a whole piece" to beaten or turned work, and supposes the instruments straight rather than curved — like the one carved on Titus's arch at Rome and those on Egyptian monuments, differing thereby from the crooked horn or keren. Gill borrows Josephus for measurements: barely a cubit long, with a narrow tube widening at the mouthpiece to receive breath, and finishing in a bell. Henry simply thinks their outline much like our own. Clarke suspects the pair differed in length and width, and so in pitch, since a distinct tone would tell hearers at once whether princes or people were summoned; Josephus, he reports, kept one for calling the nobles and the other for assembling the congregation.

Why exactly two were ordered nobody disputes. Gill, Wesley and Henry all answer from the priesthood: Aaron had fathered two sons, Eleazar and Ithamar, and each blower needed an instrument. Henry contrasts Solomon's dedication, where a hundred and twenty priests sounded together; Wesley likewise observes that the tally rose afterwards as the priestly families multiplied. Gill adds a small dispute over the funding — the Targum of Jonathan reads the command as charging Moses personally, though Gill judges it likelier the treasury bore the cost. Clarke raises the difficulty that two instruments seem far too few for so vast an army, and answers that those within earshot moved first and taught the rest in succession; he notes too that Joshua's seven trumpets were of rams' horns, not silver.

Calvin files the whole ordinance under the First Commandment. Israel was to be set moving by these blasts wherever they went, so that neither warfare nor peaceful business might be undertaken except under divine guidance and auspices. Three occasions govern their use: summoning people or rulers to public gatherings, arming them against enemies, and announcing sacrifices and festivals.

Assigning trumpeting duty to priests might look undignified, and Calvin admits the appearance before overturning it. God meant thereby to awaken deeper reverence, since priestly authority would precede every national act. Theirs was no servile errand, blowing at another man's bidding; rather they were placed above public business, lest the multitude convene tumultuously in blind and headlong passion. Earthly counsels are often debated confidently without reference to God's word, whereas this arrangement testified that every assembly over which he did not preside stood accursed. Heathen peoples had their own preliminaries, watching birds or inspecting entrails, since natural reason acknowledged that nothing prospers without help from above; Israel was bound differently, gathering at what amounted to a summons from heaven. Even the venue carried that meaning, since standing at the entrance placed them under God's eye.

Henry finds the divine authorship of so small a matter the most striking thing. Ordinary prudence might have suggested trumpets without revelation; yet Israel's constitution was to be divine throughout, so even this trifle came by command. Both he and Gill hear the gospel in the metal. Ministers are to lift up their voice like a trumpet, exposing men's sins, calling them to Christ, proclaiming release to Satan's prisoners and gathering worshippers — and the note must stay distinct, suited to whether hearers are convinced, humbled, consoled, exhorted, reproved or taught.
3:
Two blasts differ, and everything here depends on telling them apart. Gill describes the summoning note as even and continuous, produced by Aaron's sons on both instruments together, whereas a single trumpet — or, he allows, a single sounding — gathered the princes only. Ellicott hesitates over that clause. It may mean "with one trumpet", or equally "but once", or even "at the same time"; some interpreters read it as requiring both instruments simultaneously, yielding one uniform note that was nevertheless not continuous.

What the alarm actually sounded like divides them further. Gill hears something broken, uneven and quavering, and reaches for the old onomatopoeia, tara-tan-tara. Clarke agrees on the roughness — short, sharp, broken notes closing with long ones, played on both instruments at once — and thinks the resemblance between the Hebrew teruah and the Roman taratantara suggests the clarion's blare. Ellicott takes the opposite view, holding teruah to be a loud unbroken blast, distinguished from the convocation signal precisely by volume and continuity. Keil and Delitzsch draw the contrast at the level of the verbs: one term denotes blowing in short sharp bursts, the other a sustained peal.

Which camp answered which signal is spelled out only half way. Ellicott observes that the marching order had been laid down more fully two chapters earlier, and that here only the eastern and southern divisions receive instructions. Clarke reconstructs the missing arithmetic: one alarm launched the east, two the south, three presumably the west and four the north — likelier, he argues, than a single blast serving every division with brief pauses between. Wesley reads the phrase about journeys as making each blast a signal for one squadron to advance and, by consequence, for the rest to follow.

Whether the text has lost anything is a question Clarke pursues at length. The Greek version supplies a third alarm for the seaward camps and a fourth for those northward, and Clarke reports the evidence honestly: neither the Samaritan nor any version but the Coptic acknowledges the sentence, and the collations of Kennicott and De Rossi turn up nothing supporting it. Houbigant nevertheless judged the supplement so necessary that he printed the Latin in his own text and supplied Hebrew for it beneath, supposing the words original but lost to a copyist whose eye was dazzled by so many similar phrases crowded into a single verse. Ellicott quotes the same Greek addition without endorsing it.

Convocation, by contrast, wanted no alarm at all. Keil and Delitzsch note the prohibition plainly: to gather the assembly they were to blow, not to sound the war-note. Gill fixes both the venue and the purpose — the people came to the entrance of the tent, rather than moving off in separate bodies one behind another.

Ellicott presses the practical moral of that distinction further than anyone else. A clear and intelligible difference had to separate the call bringing princes or congregation to the door from the signal that struck the tents; and just so, he argues, the gospel trumpet must never yield an uncertain sound, but is to be handled faithfully and diligently by spiritual watchmen — whether the business in hand is warning the ungodly, rousing the careless, or speaking to the hearts of God's own people.
8:
Only priests might handle these instruments, and the commentators explain both the restriction and its loosening. Gill counts two blowers because Aaron had two sons, then jumps to Solomon's dedication with its hundred and twenty priests and as many trumpets, citing Maimonides for the rule that the number never fell below two nor rose above that figure. Ellicott qualifies the priestly monopoly from the later histories: usually the hazozerah belonged to priests, yet passages in Kings and Chronicles show Levites handling it, and perhaps men who were neither. Numbers grew under David and Solomon, and Josephus credits Solomon with two hundred thousand, made, he says, according to the command of Moses.

Keil and Delitzsch explain why the manner of use, and not merely the manufacture, came under divine prescription. These were instruments for the congregation's holy business, so God settled how they should serve; they belonged to the priests alone, and were to remain an everlasting statute among Israel's families, preserved and employed in all future generations by his appointment. Their blast had one governing purpose: bringing Israel to remembrance before the Lord, in wartime and at the feasts alike.

Warfare comes first, and its attached promise is generous. Keil and Delitzsch render the clause as bringing themselves to remembrance before Jehovah and being saved by him from their foes, and distinguish the idiom for entering upon war from the different phrase used elsewhere for mustering and marching out to battle. Gill defines the oppressor concretely: an invader who enters the land, besieges its cities and distresses its inhabitants. Clarke reads the summons as convening deliberation and prayer together, and concludes that whenever Israel decamped, encamped, fought or kept festival at God's appointment, signalled by his priests, they might look for both his presence and his blessing. Wesley adds the condition without which the ceremony is empty: they shall be saved if they use this ordinance trusting and depending upon God for help.

Ellicott traces the practice through the histories and marks one instructive exception. Phinehas carried these alarm-trumpets in the Midianite war, and Abijah, haranguing Jeroboam, laid great weight on Judah having the priests with them and the trumpets of alarm in their hands. At Jericho, however, the seven circling priests bore the ram's horn, not the silver instrument — a different implement for a different occasion.

Festivals close the list. Gill takes the day of gladness for any occasion of extraordinary deliverance turned into rejoicing, instancing on Aben Ezra's authority Purim and Hezekiah's seven days. Ellicott points to Solomon's dedication and Hezekiah's cleansing of the temple, and would render the closing words "before your God, even before me, Jehovah your God". Keil and Delitzsch distinguish the categories — a day of gladness being any on which joy found practical expression in sacrifice, the appointed feasts being those catalogued later, and new moons not strictly festivals except the seventh.

Calvin gets the sharpest point out of the arrangement. God thereby made plain that he approved no festival and accepted no sacrifice unless his own command went before it; the people could not choose this day or that, since prescribing them lay with the ministers of holy things. He had indeed appointed new moons and the other solemnities himself, but because men are forever daring in their innovations he would have their lawful observance ratified by trumpet-blast, as though he published the holy assemblies through priestly mouths. Calvin also prefers "your prosperities" to the usual rendering of the second offering, the name Israel gave to thanksgivings after rescue from great danger or extraordinary blessing; and he explains the memorial as meaning that when they assembled at his command he would look upon them and honour them with fatherly favour. Wesley says as much in a sentence: God takes pleasure in our religious exercises when we take pleasure in them, and holy work should be done with holy joy.
11:
How long Israel had camped beneath Sinai gets three answers, all close and none identical. Gill dates the departure to the twentieth of Ijar in the second year from Egypt and reckons the stay at twelve months less ten days, citing Jarchi and other Jewish writers, Aben Ezra saying only nearly a year. Clarke makes it eleven months and twenty days. Ellicott computes eleven months and nineteen days, assuming they pitched there on the first day of the third month — then undercuts his own figure, since Exodus names no day of that month, and he refuses to lean on the rabbinic tradition dating the law fifty days after the exodus.

Clarke notices what the Samaritan copy does here: it inserts the sentence Deuteronomy preserves, that they had dwelt long enough in this mountain and should turn and take their journey. Henry, reaching the same text independently, hears a warning against lingering. Sinai gendereth to bondage and stands for the law given there, a schoolmaster bringing us to Christ; yet no one may settle down in it, since happiness comes by promise rather than statute.

The signal itself is described with attention to the labour it set going. Henry supposes the cloud lifted and hung waiting until the tribes were ready, for striking every tent and packing every household's goods was no small business — though each family worked at its own and all at once, so many hands made quick work. Keil and Delitzsch treat the verse as a heading rather than narrative: with preparations complete the cloud rose from the tent of witness, Israel broke up in the order laid down two chapters back, and the statement that it settled in Paran summarises a whole journey whose particulars follow later, Paran being in fact the third station, not the first.

Calvin weighs their compliance and finds it short-lived. They deserve praise for setting out promptly at God's command, and the march was short — three days, as the chapter will say — yet even that harassed and wearied them, and presently, the spirit of perseverance failing, their levity and inconstancy showed itself. He also disputes a rendering: where Jerome turned the repeated noun into "troops", Calvin objects that its root is the very verb beside it, and that Scripture uses it consistently for stations or halting-places, so the phrase describes their whole progress stage by stage.

Henry finds a purpose in how insistently the chapter repeats that they moved at the Lord's commandment. Some think it written to forestall the later slander that Israel wandered so long because they had lost themselves and could not find the way out. Nothing of the kind: at every stage and step they were under divine direction, and if they did not know where they stood, he who led them knew. Those who surrender themselves to the guidance of God's word and Spirit hold a steady course even when they appear bewildered, for while they cannot lose their guide they need not fear losing their road. Gill makes the mechanism explicit: the command came in the lifting of the cloud.

Where they arrived is easier to name than place. Clarke counts three stations between Sinai and Paran, Kibroth-hattaavah and Hazeroth preceding it, and admits how hard identification is, since one often cannot tell whether a site lies forward of the last or behind it. Ellicott suspects the spot is Kibroth-hattaavah at the southern tip of Paran, and sketches that desert's limits — Canaan northward, the Arabah eastward, Sinai southward, the brook of Egypt westward — noting that Deuteronomy calls it great and terrible and that Israel kept to its eastern half. Wesley observes that they afterwards travelled elsewhere and came back to it. Henry draws the moral: every removal here is only from one wilderness into another, the changes we expect to better us often do not, and rest belongs to heaven.
14:
Calvin lays out the whole formation before commenting on it. Every Israelite except the Levites belonged to one of four hosts, each headed by a tribe with two others under its command. At every halt those standards ringed the sanctuary and the ark from the four quarters, while on the road the Levites bearing the dismantled dwelling, each family under its own load, marched interspersed among the divisions. The ark itself, carried on Levite shoulders, went before the entire column, so that everyone might follow the more confidently with God visibly showing the way. Nahshon commanded the leading host, Elizur the second, Elishama the third, Ahiezer the fourth.

Why Judah heads the column rather than Reuben interests Calvin most. Precedence here anticipates Jacob's dying oracle: descendants of the firstborn would never have surrendered their standing had God not transferred the right by that prophecy. Sovereignty did not belong to Judah until David's day, but God meant a single spark to glow amid thick darkness, cherishing hope of the promised salvation, so that this tribe's dignity might in time draw all the rest into obedience. How perverse most of them proved, Calvin adds, appeared later when they fought that decree by rejecting David. Gill hears the same note in the arrangement — Judah led the van because Israel's chief ruler, the Messiah, was to spring from it, a king gone before his people fighting their battles.

Calvin follows the other placements through the same prophecy. Reuben took second rank, which softened his disgrace; Manasseh's subordination to Ephraim fulfilled another clause of Jacob's blessing; and Dan received the fourth standard, apparently because Jacob had said that Dan should judge his people, an expression denoting pre-eminence. Perhaps, he concedes, the four leading tribes were chosen for strength and population. Even so, unless Reuben and Manasseh had been thoroughly persuaded that their demotion came by divine command, jealousy would never have let them submit calmly to men who by ordinary reckoning were their inferiors. Their self-restraint therefore deserves praise, since voluntary subjection held them in bounds without any force being applied; and Moses records that this happened not once but throughout the whole journey, the encampment always so ordered that no quarrel disturbed it.

The Levites' place is what Ellicott sets out most precisely. Chapter two had ruled that their camp should move in the midst; here the three families receive exact positions. Gershonites with their curtains and hangings and two wagons, and Merarites with the heavier framework and four, went immediately behind the eastern division of Judah, Issachar and Zebulun — the point being to give them time to raise the dwelling before the Kohathites arrived carrying the sacred things. Reuben's southern division followed, then the Kohathites in the very centre, then the western division of Ephraim, Manasseh and Benjamin, and finally Dan, Asher and Naphtali as rearguard. That sequence, which Clarke sets out as a bare table, explains for Ellicott the psalm praying God to stir up his strength before Ephraim, Benjamin and Manasseh.

Gill watches the dismantling and reads it. Levites took the structure down, as Aben Ezra says, beginning the moment the cloud was seen rising and Judah's camp began forming up, and only after Aaron and his sons had removed and wrapped the holy vessels. He finds two emblems in the operation: the eventual dismantling of the Jewish church-state with the abolition of sanctuary service, and the shifting condition of the gospel church in its own wilderness, which never stays in one place but is carried from region to region by ministers of the word, whom the Levites represent. At Reuben's standard he plays on the name, which means behold the son: with the tabernacle borne ahead of that division and the holy things behind it, whichever way the camp faced it had in view a type of Christ the Son of God, the ark being faith's object.
21:
Why the two Levite contingents travelled so far apart is Wesley's concern. Gershon and Merari moved off directly behind the leading camp, keeping a good interval ahead of Kohath, precisely so that they might have the dwelling ready to receive its furniture when the Kohathites came up some while later. Gill fixes the Kohathite position in the column: behind Reuben's standard and in front of Ephraim's, midway through the whole array. Ephraim's own division came next after them, Gill notes, with Manasseh and Benjamin ranged beneath that standard.

Dan's place at the tail is defended rather than merely reported. Gill calls that division fittest for the duty because, after Judah leading the van, it was the most populous; and he prefers a second sense for the word usually rendered rearward — gatherer-up of all the camps. Under its protection came everyone the marching tribes had left unaccounted for: males below twenty who never entered the muster rolls, women, children, the sick and the feeble, the mixed multitude, and any who straggled behind. Asher and Naphtali marched beneath the same standard, commanded, as Gill notes, by the same officers named at the earlier muster — Ahiezer over Dan, Pagiel over Asher, Ahira over Naphtali.

Gill closes the muster by totalling it. Following Jarchi, he treats the passage as describing a settled practice rather than one day's movement — the order in which Israel marched throughout — and calls the resulting formation wise, beautiful and regular. Judah's camp opened the march with 186,400 fighting men; behind them rolled the six wagons of Gershon and Merari carrying the bulkier fabric; Reuben's 151,450 followed; then Kohath with the holy things upon their shoulders; then Ephraim's 108,100; and finally Dan's 157,600, responsible for everyone unfit to march with the rest. The arithmetic matters to him as much as the sequence, since the two Levite trains are placed by what they carried — six wagons for the fabric that could be wheeled, shoulders for the sacred vessels that could not. In that whole spectacle Gill sees the church militant pictured: a body walking by gospel order and keeping all its ordinances, which he thinks a lovely sight to behold. Ellicott adds a small grammatical preference at the same verse, reading the closing words as a plain statement, and they set forward, rather than a temporal clause.
29:
Who Hobab was divides the commentators sharply. Calvin calls it a gross error to identify him with Jethro, who had gone home only days after visiting Moses: decrepit old age suits ill with such labours, Moses himself was eighty and far younger than his father-in-law, and Judges settles the matter by showing Hobab's descendants still alive in Canaan. On his reconstruction the old man, departing, left this vigorous son behind as a companion, one whose neighbourhood made the desert familiar to him. Wesley reasons identically — Raguel, Reuel and Jethro being one man under three names, Hobab must be his son, young enough for such travelling where his father was not. Henry agrees, comparing the arrangement to Barzillai leaving Chimham with David, and notes that a single Hebrew word covers both father-in-law and brother-in-law.

Ellicott works the philology harder and reaches a different result. Ordinary Hebrew syntax makes Hobab, not Jethro, the relation named here, and Judges calls him so expressly; since the cognate noun serves for any near connection by marriage, brother-in-law may be the sense. Against those who make Zipporah Hobab's daughter he urges chronology: more than forty years had passed since Moses left Egypt, and a man past eighty would naturally seek his guide among Zipporah's own generation rather than the one above hers. Whether Hobab had come with Jethro to Sinai and stayed on, or whether Israel was already passing through territory where he ranged as a nomad chief, Ellicott declines to decide. Clarke, for his part, suspects the whole episode stands out of its chronological place.

What Moses actually offered is agreed. Henry hears him staking everything on a promise — come and share our fortunes, for God has spoken good concerning Israel — and draws the rule that pilgrims bound for the heavenly Canaan should invite their friends along, since we lose none of the covenant's treasures by others coming in to share them. Clarke makes the invitation a test of religion itself. True religion is always benevolent; those who know most of God's goodness are the readiest to invite others into it; and a religion that shuts everyone out of salvation who will not hold a particular creed or worship in a particular way is not of God — witness Moses, who thought even Hobab the Arab might receive what God had promised Israel, provided he walked the same road. Ellicott turns the scene the same way, reading Moses as mouthpiece of the Jewish church and his invitation as a standing lesson to the Christian one, whose members are bound and privileged alike to pass on the summons they have themselves obeyed. Henry notes what Moses undertook in return — whatever good the Lord did to Israel they would do to him — and observes that we can give only what we receive, promising no more than to do good as God enables us, while those who share the labours of God's people share their comforts and honours too.

Why the offer failed is where Henry and Calvin converge. Henry blames affection for native air and soil, unchecked by any believing regard for the promise: Hobab sprang from Abraham's loins, the Midianites descending from him by Keturah, but he was no heir of Abraham's faith, and the visible things of this world drew him more strongly than the unseen things of the next. Calvin generalises further. Hobab shows us the whole race in a mirror, longing for what the carnal senses grasp; men naturally prefer their own country however barren, as the proverb about the rocky Ithaca of Ulysses attests, and set their affections on the present life. Calvin adds one observation in Hobab's favour, though: since Moses could not carry him at once, and only prevailed after persevering entreaty, the request for dismissal was evidently no feint.
30:
Hobab's refusal sounds final, and every commentator suspects it was not. Gill calls the answer peremptory, a man at a point for the present, yet thinks he probably changed his mind afterwards, like the son in the parable who said he would not go and went. Wesley allows that Hobab may have spoken sincerely and still been overcome later by Moses' persuasions. Clarke argues from the sequel: the urgency of what follows, together with passages in Judges and Samuel showing Hobab's descendants settled among Israel in Canaan, makes it likely he either relented or went home and returned. Ellicott concedes the narrative never says, thinks the renewed solicitation most probably succeeded, and rests on the certainty that the Kenites as a body went up with the children of Judah and dwelt among the people. Clarke turns the moment on the reader: one almost persuaded to take Christ with his cross and his reproach, and then purposing to go back to his own land and kindred, should consider what that land is — a place of destruction, whose children are hastening to perdition, so that whoever is not of Christ's kindred perishes at the brightness of his appearing.

Why a man was wanted when a cloud was leading is the obvious objection, and Clarke states it before answering. The pillar directed the general marches, not the particular excursions; parties went off on errands of their own while the main army lay still, and for those a man who knew the desert was needed — one who could point out where water lay and where fuel might be gathered. What men cannot do for themselves God does by special mercy; what he has qualified a man to do he leaves that man to do. He could have shown them the springs himself, but Hobab could show them, so let Hobab be employed — and let Hobab understand, for his encouragement, that in serving others within the course of God's providence he secures his own best interests. Clarke notes in passing that the Greek version renders the clause quite differently, making Hobab an elder among them rather than eyes to them.

Wesley and Ellicott fill in the same argument from different angles. Wesley lists what local knowledge would supply — conveniences of water for the cattle, and warning of danger from serpents, wild beasts or hostile neighbours — and offers a second possibility, that Moses wanted counsel on great and difficult matters, since guidance from God never excluded advice from men, as Jethro's own case had shown; probably, he adds, this was a wise son of a wise father. Ellicott draws the general principle: for all the direct guidance vouchsafed from heaven and the miracles they experienced, Moses neglected none of the ordinary precautions a leader owes his people, the cloud fixing route and halting-place while a desert-bred guide met the difficulties that arose along the way.

Calvin reads the clause backwards and accuses everyone else of missing it. Where others translate simply "for thou hast known", as though Moses wanted Hobab retained for Israel's convenience, Calvin insists the Hebrew carries more than one causal particle, so that the sense is not prospective but retrospective. Hobab had already known all their halting-places and served them as eyes; he had borne many inconveniences precisely in order to receive his recompense in the end. Why, Moses is asking, have you endured so much in guiding our course, unless it was to enjoy the rest along with us? On that construction the plea is not "be our eyes hereafter" but "do not throw away what your labour has earned", and Moses urges him forward by reminding him that the reward now lies close at hand. Gill adds why the promise that follows is stated twice over: the repetition confirms it, assuring Hobab the more strongly of what was pledged.
33:
Why Sinai earns the title mount of the Lord two of them answer alike. Gill points to the descent and the giving of the law there, quoting the Targums: the mount on which the glory of the divine Majesty was revealed. Calvin agrees the name fits nowhere else so well; he grants it had been so called by anticipation before the law was published, but holds the title was properly imposed afterwards, to inspire lasting reverence for what was given there. Henry marks the leave-taking rather than the name: they departed from the mountain where they had seen God's glory and been taken into covenant, never to see such appearances constantly, and Scripture scarcely mentions Sinai again except in retrospect.

Whether the three days ran consecutively is disputed outright. Calvin understands a continuous march, since no tents were pitched until Paran and the people slept in the open air. Gill breaks the reckoning up. They travelled three days before the cloud settled so as to abide, though it halted for food and sleep; the Targum of Jonathan makes the day's march thirty-six miles, yet Bunting places Kibroth-hattaavah only eight miles from Sinai. Gill therefore separates the stages — first to Taberah, a month; then to Hazeroth, seven days; then to the wilderness of Paran, where the cloud rested. Wesley takes a middle course: continued journeys with little pauses for sleep and refreshment.

Where the ark travelled is the chapter's hardest question: the marching order puts it in the middle, this verse in front. Clarke resolves it by sequence rather than position: the Kohathites carried it in the centre, but since the army never stirred until the cloud lifted, the ark is said to go before as the first thing to move. Wesley separates camp from column — in station it stood in the midst, on march it went ahead — and adds that the ark could not have served as a visible guide anyway, carried as it was on men's shoulders; the cloud always over it made ark and cloud one token of God's presence, so the leading is credited to the ark through the cloud. Calvin denies any question of distance: the ark was not sent three days ahead, but so placed in the van that when the cloud settled they halted at a station God had prescribed — which is what searching out a resting-place means. Wesley calls the phrase metaphorical, since the ark could not search and God had no need to.

Ellicott lays both sides out before choosing. From the Kohathite charge and their place behind the second camp it has been inferred that the ark travelled in the midst, and the objection that the guiding cloud rested upon it can be met by supposing the cloud spread over the whole host as a shield from the heat. Yet the natural sense of this verse is that the ark went in front, confirmed for him by Exodus, Deuteronomy, and above all the Jordan crossing, where Israel was told to follow after the ark and the same verb is used of its passing over before them. He will not conclude its place was uniform on every march, admits the earlier verse stays difficult through the ambiguity of the word for sanctuary, and reports Ibn Ezra's opinion that this three days' journey differed from all the rest in where the ark was carried.

Gill widens the cloud beyond the sanctuary. It lay not only over tabernacle and ark but spread across the whole body of the people, screening them from the sun's heat as well as guiding them and betokening the divine presence. Wesley catches an omission and makes it a rule of reading: the text says by day, but night is meant too, stated earlier — so we must compare passage with passage and supply out of one what another leaves out, as with any author.
35:
The prayer at the ark's setting out is read as a war-cry. Clarke puts the necessity bluntly: unless God arose and scattered his enemies there was no hope of Israel getting through the wilderness at all, and unless he went first they could not safely follow. Calvin explains why such a petition was needed at every departure. The march was anything but peaceful, attack was constantly to be dreaded, and Moses both begged God to go out as though armed for battle and kept up the people's courage, lest some nearer cause of terror leave them sluggish and inert. The sense, on his paraphrase, is not merely show us the road but open it by the power of thy hand.

Whose enemies they are matters most to Calvin. Moses calls them God's rather than Israel's, so that the people might know they fought under his auspices; victory could be the more confidently expected with the righteous avenger of iniquity defending his own quarrel, and there was no slight comfort in learning that whoever rose to harass them unjustly had made an enemy of the God who guards his people as the apple of his eye. That is why the psalmist afterwards borrowed the words, arming the church with confidence and keeping it cheerful under violent assault. Calvin then guards the image: Moses was not so foolish as to address the ark itself, but asked God to prove in effect that the ark was a living representation of his power and glory. Keil and Delitzsch make the same connection from the other side — Moses could speak so because he knew Jehovah and the ark were inseparable, and saw in it, as the throne of God, a material pledge of the Almighty's gracious presence; the words are recorded both as evidence of his own joyous confidence and as encouragement to the congregation to share it.

The prayer at the halt admits more than one construction. Gill offers three. It may ask that God, the ark being at rest, would take up his abode among them and manifest his love and mercy; or, rendered actively, that he would return the many thousands of Israel to the land sworn to their fathers — Ben Gersom's reading, who explains the word return by the patriarchs who had dwelt there; or it may be a petition that God would turn those thousands into myriads and multiply them tenfold, which is how the Jerusalem Targum takes it, praying him to bless the myriads and multiply the thousands of the children of Israel. Clarke prefers to date the utterance rather than parse it — these were the words spoken at the moment the divisions halted to pitch — notes that the Hebrew is literally the ten thousand thousands, and thinks the sixty-eighth psalm composed with reference to this history, though David applied it to bringing the ark up to Jerusalem.

Calvin finds a pastoral purpose in the second prayer that the first did not need. By praying so, Moses was also exhorting the people to patience, lest weariness at the delay breed indignation; a protracted journey meant arriving later at their rest, and their minds were plainly exasperated, as though slower progress were a kind of cheat. To correct that impatience he reminds them their halts did them good, since God, staying at home like the head of a family, could then show his care of them — the comparison being to a man who uses a spell of rest and release from other business to give himself unreservedly to his own household. Clarke draws the matching conclusion: without ark and cloud they had neither direction nor safety on the move, and neither rest nor comfort when stationary, so that the word of God and the Spirit of God are equally necessary to every follower of Christ through all the changes of this mortal life.
